danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 21
paragraphs: Pierre måtte som en af hovedgæsterne sætte sig til boston sammen med grev Rostov, generalen og obersten. Ved kortbordet kom han til at sidde lige over for Natásha og blev slået af en ejendommelig forandring, der var sket med hende siden ballet. Hun var tavs og ikke blot mindre køn end ved ballet, men reddede sig kun fra at se almindelig ud ved sit blik af mild ligegyldighed over for alt omkring hende.

»Hvad er der med hende?« tænkte Pierre og kiggede på hende. Hun sad ved siden af sin søster ved tebordet og svarede modvilligt, uden at se på ham, på noget Boris sagde, da han satte sig ved siden af hende. Efter at have spillet en hel farve ud og til sin partners glæde taget fem stik kiggede Pierre, der hørte hilsener og skridt fra én, der var kommet ind i stuen, mens han samlede sine stik op, igen på Natásha.
»Hvad er der dog sket med hende?« spurgte han sig selv med endnu større undren.

Fyrst Andrej stod foran hende og sagde noget til hende med et blik af øm omsorg. Hun havde løftet hovedet og så op på ham, rødmende og tydeligvis kæmpende for at beherske sin hurtige vejrtrækning. Og den klare glød fra en indre ild, der havde været undertrykt, blussede igen op i hende. Hun var fuldstændig forvandlet, og fra en kedelig pige var hun igen blevet det, hun havde været ved ballet.
Fyrst Andrej gik hen til Pierre, og Pierre lagde mærke til et nyt og ungdommeligt udtryk i sin vens ansigt.
Pierre byttede plads flere gange under spillet og sad snart med ryggen til Natásha, snart med ansigtet mod hende, men under alle seks rubbere iagttog han hende og sin ven.
»Der foregår noget meget vigtigt mellem dem,« tænkte Pierre, og en følelse, der var på én gang glad og smertefuld, rørte ham og fik ham til at forsømme spillet.

Efter seks rubbere rejste generalen sig og sagde, at det ingen mening havde at spille på den måde, og Pierre blev befriet. Natásha sad på den ene side og talte med Sonja og Boris, og Véra sagde noget til fyrst Andrej med et fint smil. Pierre gik hen til sin ven, spurgte om de talte om hemmeligheder og satte sig ved siden af dem. Véra, der havde lagt mærke til fyrst Andrejs opmærksomhed mod Natásha, havde besluttet, at ved et selskab — et rigtigt aftenselskab — var fine hentydninger til den ømme passion absolut nødvendige. Hun greb et øjeblik, da fyrst Andrej var alene, og begyndte en samtale med ham om følelser i almindelighed og om sin søster. Over for en så intellektuel gæst, som hun anså fyrst Andrej for at være, følte hun, at hun måtte anvende al sin diplomatiske takt.
Da Pierre gik hen til dem, bemærkede han, at Véra blev revet med af sin selvtilfredse tale, mens fyrst Andrej virkede forlegen — noget der sjældent skete for ham.

»Hvad mener De?« sagde Véra med et underfundigt smil. »De er så skarptseende, fyrste, og forstår menneskers karakter så godt ved første blik. Hvad synes De om Natalie? Kunne hun være standhaftig i sine tilbøjeligheder? Kunne hun ligesom andre kvinder« (Véra mente sig selv) »elske en mand én gang for alle og forblive tro mod ham for evigt? Det er, hvad jeg anser for sand kærlighed. Hvad mener De, fyrste?«

»Jeg kender Deres søster for lidt,« svarede fyrst Andrej med et sarkastisk smil, hvorunder han ønskede at skjule sin forlegenhed, »til at kunne løse et så delikat spørgsmål, og desuden har jeg bemærket, at jo mindre tiltalende en kvinde er, desto mere standhaftig er hun tilbøjelig til at være,« tilføjede han og så op på Pierre, der netop nærmede sig.

»Ja, det er sandt, fyrste. I vore dage,« fortsatte Véra — idet hun nævnte »vore dage«, som folk med begrænset forstand gerne gør, fordi de bilder sig ind at have opdaget og vurderet de særlige træk ved »vore dage«, og at menneskelige egenskaber forandrer sig med tiderne — »i vore dage har en pige så megen frihed, at fornøjelsen ved at blive gjort kur til ofte kvæler den ægte følelse i hende. Og man må indrømme, at Natalie er meget modtagelig.« Denne venden tilbage til emnet Natásha fik fyrst Andrej til at rynke brynene i ubehag; han var ved at rejse sig, men Véra fortsatte med et endnu finere smil:

»Jeg tror, ingen har haft flere bejlere end hun,« fortsatte hun, »men indtil for ganske nylig har hun aldrig for alvor interesseret sig for nogen. Nu ved De, greve,« sagde hun til Pierre, »selv vores kære fætter Boris, som — det bliver mellem os — var langt inde i ømhedens land...« (hun hentydede til et kærlighedskort, der var meget på mode dengang).
Fyrst Andrej rynkede panden og forblev tavs.
»De er ven med Boris, ikke sandt?« spurgte Véra.
»Jo, jeg kender ham...«
»Jeg formoder, han har fortalt Dem om sin barndomsforelskelse i Natásha?«
»Åh, var der tale om barndomsforelskelse?« spurgte fyrst Andrej pludselig og rødmede uventet.
»Ja, De ved, mellem fætre og kusiner fører fortrolighed ofte til kærlighed. Le cousinage est un dangereux voisinage. * Synes De ikke?«
* »Slægtskab er et farligt naboskab.«

»Åh, bestemt!« sagde fyrst Andrej, og med pludselig og unaturlig livlighed begyndte han at drille Pierre med, at han måtte passe meget på med sine halvtredsårige moskovitiske kusiner. Midt i disse spøgende bemærkninger rejste han sig, tog Pierre under armen og trak ham til side.
»Nå?« spurgte Pierre, overrasket over sin vens mærkelige ophidselse og det blik, han kastede på Natásha, da han rejste sig.

»Jeg må... jeg må tale med dig,« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Du kender det par damehandsker?« (Han hentydede til frimurer-handskerne, der gives til en nyoptaget broder, som han skal forære den kvinde, han elsker.) »Jeg... men nej, jeg taler med dig senere,« og med et sælsomt lys i øjnene og en uro i sine bevægelser nærmede fyrst Andrej sig Natásha og satte sig ved siden af hende. Pierre så, hvordan fyrst Andrej spurgte hende om noget, og hvordan hun rødmede, da hun svarede.
Men i det øjeblik kom Berg hen til Pierre og insisterede på, at han skulle deltage i en diskussion mellem generalen og obersten om forholdene i Spanien.

Berg var tilfreds og lykkelig. Smilet af fornøjelse forlod aldrig hans ansigt. Selskabet var en stor succes og lignede ganske andre selskaber, han havde set. Alt var det samme: damernes fine samtale, kortene, generalen der hævede stemmen ved kortbordet, og samovaren og tekagerne. Kun én ting manglede, som han altid havde set ved de aftenselskaber, han ønskede at efterligne. De havde endnu ikke haft en højrøstet samtale blandt mændene og en diskussion om noget vigtigt og klogt. Nu var generalen begyndt en sådan diskussion, og Berg trak Pierre hen til den.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre, as one of the principal guests, had to sit down to boston with Count Rostov, the general, and the colonel. At the card table he happened to be sitting directly across from Natasha, and was struck by a curious change that had come over her since the ball. She was quiet, and not only less pretty than at the ball, but saved from plainness only by her expression of gentle indifference to everything around her.

"What's the matter with her?" thought Pierre, glancing at her. She was sitting beside her sister at the tea table and reluctantly, without looking at him, responded to Boris, who had sat down next to her. After playing out a whole suit and, to his partner's delight, taking five tricks, Pierre heard greetings and footsteps as someone entered the room while he was gathering his cards. He glanced again at Natasha.
"What has happened to her?" he asked himself with even greater surprise.

Prince Andrew was standing before her, saying something to her with a look of tender concern. She had raised her head and was gazing up at him, flushed and clearly trying to control her rapid breathing. And the bright glow of some inner fire that had been suppressed was burning in her again. She was completely transformed — from a plain girl back into what she had been at the ball.
Prince Andrew went up to Pierre, and Pierre noticed a new and youthful expression on his friend's face.
Pierre changed seats several times during the game — sitting now with his back to Natasha, now facing her — but throughout all six rubbers he kept watching her and his friend.
"Something very important is happening between them," thought Pierre, and a feeling that was both joyful and painful stirred in him and made him neglect the game.

After six rubbers the general got up, declaring it was no use playing like that, and Pierre was free. Natasha was on one side of the room talking with Sonya and Boris, and Vera was saying something to Prince Andrew with a knowing smile. Pierre went up to his friend and, asking whether they were sharing secrets, sat down beside them. Vera, having noticed Prince Andrew's attention to Natasha, had decided that at a party — a real evening party — subtle allusions to romantic feelings were absolutely essential, and seizing a moment when Prince Andrew was alone she had started a conversation about feelings in general and about her sister. With such an intellectual guest as she considered Prince Andrew to be, she felt she needed to employ all her diplomatic skill.
When Pierre joined them he noticed that Vera was getting carried away by her own self-satisfied talk, while Prince Andrew looked embarrassed — something that rarely happened with him.

"What do you think?" Vera was saying with a sly smile. "You're so perceptive, Prince — you understand people's characters so well at a glance. What do you think of Natalie? Could she be constant in her attachments? Could she, like other women" — Vera meant herself — "love a man once and for all and remain true to him forever? That is what I consider true love. What do you think, Prince?"

"I know your sister too little," replied Prince Andrew with a sardonic smile meant to hide his discomfort, "to answer such a delicate question. And besides, I've noticed that the less attractive a woman is, the more constant she tends to be," he added, and looked up at Pierre, who was just approaching.

"Yes, that's true, Prince. In our day," continued Vera — using the phrase "our day" the way people of limited intelligence love to do, imagining they have discovered and assessed the special qualities of "our day," as if human nature changes with the times — "in our day a girl has so much freedom that the pleasure of being courted often smothers real feeling. And I must admit that Natalie is very susceptible." This return to the topic of Natasha made Prince Andrew frown uncomfortably; he was about to stand up, but Vera went on with an even subtler smile:

"I think no one has been more courted than she," she continued, "but until quite recently she never cared seriously for anyone. Now you know, Count," she said to Pierre, "even our dear cousin Boris, who between ourselves was very far gone in the land of tender feelings..." — alluding to a popular map of love that was in fashion at the time.
Prince Andrew frowned and said nothing.
"You're friendly with Boris, aren't you?" asked Vera.
"Yes, I know him..."
"I'm sure he's told you about his childhood love for Natasha?"
"Oh, there was a childhood romance?" Prince Andrew asked suddenly, blushing unexpectedly.
"Yes, you know — between cousins, closeness often leads to love. Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood, don't you think?"
* "Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood."

"Oh, absolutely!" said Prince Andrew, and with sudden, unnatural energy he began teasing Pierre about the need to be very careful with his fifty-year-old Moscow cousins. In the middle of these jokes he stood up, took Pierre by the arm, and drew him aside.
"Well?" asked Pierre, surprised by his friend's strange animation and noticing the glance he directed at Natasha as he rose.

"I must... I must talk to you," said Prince Andrew. "You know those women's gloves?" — he was referring to the Masonic gloves given to a newly initiated Brother, to be presented to the woman he loved. "I... but no, I'll tell you later..." and with a strange light in his eyes and a restlessness in his movements, Prince Andrew went over to Natasha and sat down beside her. Pierre watched as Prince Andrew asked her something and she blushed as she replied.
But at that moment Berg came up to Pierre and insisted that he join a debate between the general and the colonel about affairs in Spain.

Berg was satisfied and happy. The smile of pleasure never left his face. The party was a great success and exactly like other parties he had attended. Everything was just right: the ladies' subtle conversation, the cards, the general raising his voice at the card table, the samovar and the tea cakes. Only one thing was still missing — the thing he had always noticed at the evening parties he wanted to emulate. They hadn't yet had a loud, lively discussion among the men about something important and clever. Now the general had started just such a discussion, and so Berg pulled Pierre into it.
